traps.name: Multi-AZ is not read scaling
traps.pattern: 'Reporting queries slow down the production RDS database... improve performance' with Multi-AZ as an option
traps.spot_it: Multi-AZ standby is not readable (instance deployment). Performance/offload reads -> read replica (or Multi-AZ DB CLUSTER whose 2 standbys are readable). Multi-AZ answers only 'high availability' or 'minimize downtime during patching'.

traps.name: Read replica is not HA / failover
traps.pattern: 'Database must remain available if an AZ fails' with 'create a read replica' offered
traps.spot_it: Replicas are async and promotion is manual. Automatic failover = Multi-AZ (or Aurora replicas, which are both). Cross-Region replica is DR, still manual.

traps.name: NACL forgets the return trip
traps.pattern: 'Web servers behind a custom NACL cannot reach the internet / clients get no response' or 'allow inbound 443 only'
traps.spot_it: NACLs are stateless: add an outbound (or inbound) rule for ephemeral ports 1024-65535. A security group needs no such rule (stateful).

traps.name: Gateway endpoint is S3 + DynamoDB only
traps.pattern: 'Access SQS/Kinesis/SSM privately without NAT... use a gateway endpoint'
traps.spot_it: Only S3 and DynamoDB have gateway endpoints. Everything else = interface endpoint (PrivateLink). Also: gateway endpoints are not reachable from on-prem or peered VPCs -> interface endpoint for S3 over Direct Connect.

traps.name: Spot for stateful or must-finish workloads
traps.pattern: 'Reduce cost of the production database / message broker / long-running job that cannot be interrupted' with Spot listed
traps.spot_it: Spot can vanish with 2 minutes notice. Use only for fault-tolerant, stateless, checkpointable, batch, CI, EMR task nodes. Databases and the primary web fleet -> Reserved/Savings Plans.

traps.name: Intelligent-Tiering means UNKNOWN pattern
traps.pattern: 'Access patterns are unpredictable / unknown / change over time... minimize cost'
traps.spot_it: Unknown or changing -> Intelligent-Tiering. If the pattern IS known (accessed once a month), pick the explicit class (Standard-IA) - it is cheaper because there is no monitoring fee.

traps.name: One Zone-IA only for re-creatable data
traps.pattern: 'Infrequently accessed backups that must survive an AZ outage / critical' with One Zone-IA as the cheapest option
traps.spot_it: One Zone-IA lives in a single AZ. Cheapest only if the data can be regenerated (thumbnails, secondary copies). Critical infrequent data -> Standard-IA.

traps.name: Standard-IA 30-day minimum vs short-lived data
traps.pattern: 'Logs are needed for 7 days then deleted... move to Standard-IA after 1 day to save money'
traps.spot_it: IA/OZ-IA bill a 30-day minimum and lifecycle cannot transition to IA before 30 days in Standard. Short-lived data stays in Standard with an expiration rule. Glacier classes have 90/180-day minimums.

traps.name: Glacier Instant is not Glacier Flexible
traps.pattern: 'Archive accessed once a quarter but must be retrieved in milliseconds' vs 'retrieval within hours acceptable'
traps.spot_it: Milliseconds required -> Glacier Instant Retrieval (90-day min, higher per-GB than Flexible). Hours acceptable -> Glacier Flexible (Expedited 1-5 min, Standard 3-5 h, Bulk 5-12 h). 12-48 h and rarely -> Deep Archive.

traps.name: CloudFront vs Global Accelerator
traps.pattern: 'Improve global performance' for a TCP/UDP game server, or 'customers must allow-list a static IP'
traps.spot_it: HTTP + cacheable -> CloudFront. Non-HTTP, UDP, static anycast IPs, fast cross-Region failover, no caching -> Global Accelerator. 'Whitelist IPs' + ALB -> Global Accelerator in front of ALB (or NLB).

traps.name: NLB when static IP or non-HTTP
traps.pattern: 'Partners need a fixed IP address for firewall rules' or 'millions of TCP connections / UDP / MQTT'
traps.spot_it: ALB has no static IP and speaks only HTTP. NLB gives one Elastic IP per AZ and handles TCP/UDP/TLS at extreme scale. Need L7 routing AND static IP -> NLB -> ALB target or Global Accelerator -> ALB.

traps.name: Peering is non-transitive; TGW is
traps.pattern: 'VPC A peered to B, B peered to C; A cannot reach C' or 'connect 40 VPCs and on-prem'
traps.spot_it: Peering is strictly 1:1 - no hopping through a middle VPC. Full-mesh peering does not scale; Transit Gateway is the hub. Also peering fails with overlapping CIDRs -> PrivateLink.

traps.name: PrivateLink for one-way service exposure / overlapping CIDRs
traps.pattern: 'SaaS provider must expose an API to hundreds of customer VPCs' or 'both VPCs use 10.0.0.0/16'
traps.spot_it: Endpoint service (NLB) + interface endpoints in consumer VPCs. No peering, no route-table exposure, CIDR overlap irrelevant, one direction only. Peering/TGW would expose the whole network.

traps.name: RDS encryption only at creation
traps.pattern: 'Existing unencrypted RDS instance must be encrypted with minimal downtime'
traps.spot_it: You cannot toggle encryption on a live instance. Snapshot -> copy snapshot with KMS key -> restore new instance -> repoint. Same for EBS volumes (snapshot -> encrypted copy -> new volume). Unencrypted primary cannot have an encrypted replica.

traps.name: KMS automatic rotation only for customer-managed symmetric keys
traps.pattern: 'Enable automatic rotation' for imported key material, an asymmetric key, or an AWS-managed key
traps.spot_it: Move: pick a customer-managed symmetric key with KMS-generated material - it is the only one whose rotation you control (automatic on a configurable 90-2,560 day period, default 365, plus on-demand rotation). AWS-managed keys rotate yearly and you cannot change it. Imported material and asymmetric/HMAC keys must be rotated manually (new key + alias switch).

traps.name: SSE-KMS gives audit trail, SSE-S3 does not
traps.pattern: 'Must log every use of the encryption key / separate permissions to decrypt / rotate under company control'
traps.spot_it: Audit, key policies, cross-account or revocation -> SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key. SSE-S3 is fine for 'simply encrypt at rest'. Beware KMS request quotas at high PUT/GET rates -> S3 Bucket Keys.

traps.name: Secrets Manager rotates; Parameter Store does not
traps.pattern: 'Rotate database credentials every 30 days automatically with least overhead'
traps.spot_it: Secrets Manager has native rotation for RDS/Aurora/Redshift/DocumentDB. Parameter Store SecureString needs a custom Lambda + EventBridge to rotate. Pick Parameter Store only when cost is the driver and no rotation is required.

traps.name: SCP does not grant; it bounds
traps.pattern: 'Attach an SCP to grant developers access to X' or 'admin in member account still cannot launch in eu-west-1'
traps.spot_it: SCPs only limit. Missing permission = check identity policy. Unexpected denial for a full admin = SCP (or permission boundary / explicit deny). SCPs do not affect the management account.

traps.name: Permission boundary vs SCP scope
traps.pattern: 'Allow developers to create IAM roles but prevent privilege escalation' vs 'prevent all accounts in an OU from using a service'
traps.spot_it: Boundary = per-principal max inside an account (require iam:PermissionsBoundary on CreateRole). SCP = per-account/OU max via Organizations. Both are ceilings; neither grants.

traps.name: Session Manager replaces the bastion
traps.pattern: 'Administer private EC2 instances securely with no inbound ports / no SSH keys / audit sessions'
traps.spot_it: SSM Session Manager: IAM-controlled, logs to S3/CloudWatch, no port 22, no bastion, no key pairs. A bastion host answer is the distractor unless the question demands SSH tooling.

traps.name: IMDSv2 for SSRF
traps.pattern: 'Web application vulnerable to SSRF could leak instance role credentials'
traps.spot_it: Enforce IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required, hop limit 1) in the launch template. IMDSv2 requires a PUT to get a session token, which SSRF cannot forge.

traps.name: EFS is Linux only; FSx for Windows is SMB
traps.pattern: 'Shared file storage for Windows EC2 instances with Active Directory permissions'
traps.spot_it: EFS = NFS/POSIX for Linux. Windows/SMB/NTFS/AD -> FSx for Windows File Server. Mixed NFS+SMB -> FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

traps.name: FSx for Lustre for HPC + S3
traps.pattern: 'High-performance computing / ML training on data stored in S3, hundreds of GB/s, sub-millisecond'
traps.spot_it: FSx for Lustre links to an S3 bucket (lazy load, export). EFS Max I/O is the distractor - far lower throughput. Scratch for temp, persistent for long-lived.

traps.name: DynamoDB hot partition: fix the key, not the capacity
traps.pattern: 'Throttling on a DynamoDB table even though total provisioned capacity is not exceeded'
traps.spot_it: One partition key value (e.g., date, status) is hot. Add high-cardinality partition key or write sharding (suffix). Adding RCUs/WCUs or DAX does not fix write hot keys.

traps.name: DAX vs ElastiCache
traps.pattern: 'Reduce read latency of a DynamoDB table to microseconds with minimal code change' vs 'cache for RDS queries'
traps.spot_it: DynamoDB -> DAX (API-compatible). RDS/Aurora or arbitrary objects -> ElastiCache (needs code). ElastiCache in front of DynamoDB is a wrong-tool distractor.

traps.name: Kinesis Streams replay vs Firehose no storage
traps.pattern: 'Multiple applications consume the same clickstream; must reprocess last 7 days' vs 'load stream into S3 with least effort'
traps.spot_it: Retention/replay/multiple consumers -> Data Streams (retention up to 365 days). Just deliver to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch near-real-time -> Firehose (no storage, min 60 s buffer). Firehose cannot replay.

traps.name: SQS FIFO 300 TPS
traps.pattern: 'Strict ordering required for 5,000 messages per second'
traps.spot_it: Move: do not pick plain FIFO. FIFO caps at 300 msg/s per API action (3,000 with 10-message batching). Enable high-throughput FIFO (many message groups, thousands of msg/s per action), or switch to Kinesis Data Streams where ordering is per shard and you add shards for throughput.

traps.name: Step Functions for orchestration; SWF is legacy
traps.pattern: 'Coordinate multiple Lambda functions with retries, branching and human approval'
traps.spot_it: Step Functions (Standard for long/exactly-once, Express for high-volume short). SWF appears as the legacy distractor; SQS chains are the DIY distractor with more overhead.

traps.name: EventBridge for SaaS / cross-account / schedules / content routing
traps.pattern: 'React to events from Zendesk/Datadog', 'route events between accounts', 'run a Lambda every day at 2am'
traps.spot_it: EventBridge (partner event sources, cross-account buses, Scheduler, content filtering, archive/replay). SNS is the distractor when routing depends on event content or the source is SaaS/AWS service events.

traps.name: Aurora Global for cross-Region seconds of RPO
traps.pattern: 'Relational database must fail over to another Region within a minute with less than 1 second of data loss'
traps.spot_it: Aurora Global Database (<1 s lag, RTO <1 min). RDS cross-Region read replica has minutes of lag and manual promotion. DynamoDB global tables only if the workload is key-value.

traps.name: Snowball when the network takes more than about a week
traps.pattern: 'Migrate 100 TB over a 1 Gbps link that is also used by production' or 'within 10 days'
traps.spot_it: Move: order Snowball Edge. 1 Gbps ~ 10 TB/day at 100% utilization -> 100 TB ~ 10-12 days best case, and production traffic makes it worse. Snowball Edge Storage Optimized is 80 TB usable (210 TB on the newer variant), so parallel devices cover PB-scale - Snowmobile is discontinued and is never the answer. Snowball lands in S3 Standard, then lifecycle to Glacier.

traps.name: DataSync online vs Snow offline
traps.pattern: 'Migrate an on-prem NFS share to EFS over Direct Connect' vs 'no connectivity / weeks of transfer'
traps.spot_it: Bandwidth available and time OK -> DataSync (incremental, scheduled, 10 Gbps/agent). Bandwidth insufficient -> Snowball. Neither is continuous sync; Storage Gateway is for ongoing hybrid access.

traps.name: Storage Gateway cached vs stored
traps.pattern: 'Keep frequently accessed data on-prem with the full dataset in AWS' vs 'entire dataset must stay on-prem with low latency; back up to AWS'
traps.spot_it: Cached volumes: S3 is primary, hot subset local. Stored volumes: local disk is primary, async EBS snapshots to AWS. File Gateway for NFS/SMB to S3 objects; Tape Gateway for backup software.

traps.name: Savings Plans over RIs unless capacity reservation or resale needed
traps.pattern: 'Steady EC2 usage for 3 years; may change instance types and Regions; lowest cost'
traps.spot_it: Compute Savings Plan (flexible across family/Region/OS, covers Fargate + Lambda). Standard RI only if you need zonal capacity reservation or Marketplace resale. Convertible RI is the answer only when the question literally says 'Reserved Instance' and family may change.

traps.name: Convertible RI when the family may change
traps.pattern: 'Reserved Instances... but the team expects to move to newer instance families during the term'
traps.spot_it: Convertible RI (up to 66%, exchangeable). Standard RI locks the family (size flex only). If not constrained to RIs, a Compute Savings Plan is equivalent flexibility.

traps.name: Cost Explorer analyzes, Budgets alerts, CUR is raw
traps.pattern: 'Notify when forecasted spend exceeds 80%' vs 'analyze last 6 months by service' vs 'hourly line-item data for a BI tool'
traps.spot_it: Alert/action -> Budgets. Visualize/forecast/recommend -> Cost Explorer. Granular raw data to S3 for Athena/QuickSight -> Cost and Usage Report. Unexpected spikes -> Cost Anomaly Detection.

traps.name: Compute Optimizer for right-sizing
traps.pattern: 'Identify over-provisioned EC2/EBS/Lambda across the organization'
traps.spot_it: Compute Optimizer (ML on CloudWatch metrics). Trusted Advisor flags idle/low-utilization but Compute Optimizer gives specific instance-type recommendations. Cost Explorer rightsizing is EC2-only.

traps.name: Same-AZ free only via private IP
traps.pattern: 'Two EC2 instances in the same AZ incur data transfer charges'
traps.spot_it: They communicate over public/Elastic IPs. Use private IPs (free intra-AZ). Cross-AZ costs $0.01/GB each direction; keep chatty tiers in one AZ or accept the HA trade-off.

traps.name: Idle public IPv4 addresses are billed
traps.pattern: 'Unexpected charges for Elastic IPs that are not attached to anything' or 'reduce cost of a fleet that does not need internet ingress'
traps.spot_it: Move: release the unused Elastic IPs and stop assigning public IPv4 to instances that do not need it. Since Feb 2024 every public IPv4 address costs $0.005/hour whether attached or idle (~$3.60/mo each). Put instances in private subnets behind a NAT gateway or an ALB, or move to IPv6, instead of giving each one a public IP.

traps.name: NAT gateway data processing fee for S3/DynamoDB traffic
traps.pattern: 'High NAT gateway costs from private instances uploading to S3'
traps.spot_it: Add a gateway endpoint for S3 (and DynamoDB): traffic bypasses NAT and the endpoint is free. For other services with heavy traffic, interface endpoints ($0.01/GB) beat NAT ($0.045/GB).

traps.name: Least operational overhead: managed and serverless always win
traps.pattern: Two options both work; one uses EC2 + scripts, the other a managed service
traps.spot_it: Pick the managed/serverless one: Aurora Serverless over self-managed MySQL, Fargate over EC2 launch type, Firehose over Lambda + Kinesis consumer, Secrets Manager over cron rotation, AWS Backup over scripted snapshots, Transfer Family over SFTP on EC2.

traps.name: Lambda 15-minute / 10 GB wall
traps.pattern: 'Process runs for 45 minutes' or 'needs 32 GB of memory' with Lambda offered as serverless
traps.spot_it: Lambda caps at 15 min and 10 GB. Long or large -> Fargate task, AWS Batch, Step Functions splitting work, or EC2 Spot. Chunking work across Lambdas is valid only when the task is parallelizable.

traps.name: Health check type in ASG
traps.pattern: 'Instances pass status checks but the app is unresponsive; ASG does not replace them'
traps.spot_it: ASG default uses EC2 status checks. Enable ELB health checks on the ASG so application-level failures trigger replacement. Set grace period to cover boot time.

traps.name: Alias vs CNAME at the zone apex
traps.pattern: 'Point example.com (root domain) to an ALB / CloudFront'
traps.spot_it: CNAME is forbidden at the apex. Use an Alias record (free, health-check aware). Alias cannot target an EC2 public IP (use A record / Elastic IP).

traps.name: Cognito user pool vs identity pool
traps.pattern: 'Users sign in with Google and then upload directly to S3' vs 'protect API Gateway with user sign-in'
traps.spot_it: Authentication + JWT for API Gateway -> user pool. Temporary AWS credentials to call S3/DynamoDB directly (incl. guests) -> identity pool (federated identities). Often both: user pool authenticates, identity pool authorizes.

traps.name: Enable versioning before replication or Object Lock
traps.pattern: 'Cross-Region replication fails to enable' or 'Object Lock option greyed out'
traps.spot_it: Move: turn on versioning first - both features require it (on source AND destination for replication). Replication then copies only new objects; use S3 Batch Replication to backfill existing ones. Object Lock can now be enabled on an existing versioned bucket (since Nov 2023), but retention still applies only to objects written afterwards.

traps.name: Choose two: partial credit does not exist
traps.pattern: Multiple-response stem with five options
traps.spot_it: Pick exactly the number asked. Both must be correct; the two usually solve different halves of the requirement (e.g., one for security, one for availability). If three look right, one is a subset of another - drop it.

tips: Read the last sentence (the stem) first, extract the superlative (MOST cost-effective / LEAST operational overhead / MOST secure / highest availability / lowest latency / minimal application changes), then read the scenario hunting for constraints that filter options.

Underline the constraint nouns: 'Windows', 'POSIX', 'UDP', 'static IP', 'ordering', 'replay', 'sub-millisecond', 'cross-Region', 'no code change', 'existing licenses'. Each one maps to exactly one service in the keyword table.

Eliminate any option that violates a hard fact first (Lambda >15 min, EFS on Windows, ALB static IP, Multi-AZ for reads, Spot for a database). Usually two options die instantly; decide between the remaining two on the superlative.

When two options both work, apply the tie-breaker hierarchy the exam uses: managed/serverless > fewer moving parts > native integration > cheapest that still meets the requirement. Never pick 'more capable' if the extra capability was not asked for.

Cost questions: first check whether the requirement is being met at all (RTO, availability), then choose the cheapest survivor. The cheapest option that breaks a stated requirement is the primary trap.
Operational overhead questions: count the things you would have to patch, scale, rotate or script. Cron jobs on EC2, custom Lambda rotation, self-managed Kafka and bastion hosts all lose.

Security questions: prefer roles over keys, IAM over network-only controls, encryption in transit and at rest, least privilege, private connectivity (endpoints) over public paths, and managed detection (GuardDuty) over homegrown log parsing.
Availability questions: look for single points of failure hidden in the answer - one NAT gateway, one AZ, one instance with an Elastic IP, Memcached (no failover), instance store, single-AZ RDS.

Performance questions: identify the bottleneck layer (compute, storage IOPS, network, database reads, DNS, edge) and match the fix to that layer. Caching (CloudFront/ElastiCache/DAX) beats scaling the origin when reads dominate.

Numbers are decision gates: 'retrieve within 12 hours' allows Deep Archive, 'within 1 hour' does not; '90 days then delete' fits Glacier Flexible's 90-day minimum exactly; 'items over 400 KB' kills DynamoDB; 'runs for 45 minutes' kills Lambda. Message size is now a soft gate - the exam still tests 256 KB for SQS/SNS, but the live SQS limit is 1 MiB, so answer 256 KB unless the stem itself cites the new limit.
Multiple-response (Choose TWO): the two correct answers usually address two different sub-requirements in the scenario. Map each option to a sentence in the scenario; the orphan options are wrong.

If an option mentions a service you have never heard of, it is usually a distractor - but check that it is not the one obscure service the scenario perfectly describes (Keyspaces, Timestream, GWLB, Transfer Family, AppFlow, DataSync). Two names are now traps by definition: Snowmobile is discontinued and QLDB reached end of support in July 2025.
Do not over-engineer: 'minimal changes to the application' means keep the protocol and interface (Amazon MQ for JMS apps, FSx for SMB apps, RDS same engine, S3 File Gateway for NFS writers).
Use time boxes: 90 seconds per question on the first pass, flag anything longer, and bank the easy points. Return to flagged items with the remaining time rather than burning 5 minutes early.
Trust first instinct on flagged questions unless you find a concrete fact you missed; changing answers on vibes lowers scores.
exam_room: 130 minutes for 65 questions = 2 minutes each. Aim for 90 seconds average on pass one to leave 30 minutes for flagged items and review.
15 of the 65 questions are unscored experimental items. A bizarre or ambiguous question may be one of them - answer, flag, move on; do not let it wreck your pacing.
No penalty for guessing. Never leave a blank; on the last two minutes fill every remaining question.
Eliminate two, then decide between two. The exam is built so that two options are clearly wrong on a hard fact and two are close; spend your time on the close pair.
Multiple-response says 'Choose two' (or three). Select exactly that count - fewer or more is an automatic miss.
Flag-and-move: if you cannot see the discriminating fact in 2 minutes, choose your best guess, flag it, continue. Flagged questions often resolve after a later question reminds you of the fact.
Passing is 720/1000 scaled - roughly 70-75% raw. You can miss 13-15 scored questions and pass. One hard question is not worth panic.

Read the stem literally: 'MOST cost-effective' with 'must retrieve within milliseconds' is a different question from 'MOST cost-effective' alone. The requirement clauses are the filter; the superlative is the sort.

top_focus_8020.topic: S3 storage classes, lifecycle rules, min durations and Glacier retrieval tiers
top_focus_8020.why: Appears in every domain (cost, resilience, security via Object Lock); pure memorization of 8 classes with durations/retrieval times converts directly into 4-6 questions.

top_focus_8020.topic: RDS Multi-AZ vs read replicas vs Aurora (replicas, Global Database, Serverless v2)
top_focus_8020.why: The most repeated discrimination on the exam: HA vs read scaling vs cross-Region. Expect 4-5 questions plus RDS encryption-at-creation and Proxy.

top_focus_8020.topic: Storage picker: EBS types vs EFS vs FSx (Windows / Lustre / ONTAP) vs instance store
top_focus_8020.why: Each has a one-word trigger (Windows, POSIX, HPC, IOPS, ephemeral); 3-4 questions and nearly zero ambiguity once the triggers are memorized.

top_focus_8020.topic: Messaging picker: SQS Standard/FIFO, SNS fan-out, EventBridge, Kinesis Streams vs Firehose, Step Functions
top_focus_8020.why: Decoupling shows up in resilience and performance; limits (256 KB, 300 TPS, shard 1/2 MB, retention) are the tested facts. 4-5 questions.

top_focus_8020.topic: VPC security and connectivity: SG vs NACL, gateway vs interface endpoints, NAT cost, peering vs TGW vs PrivateLink, DX vs VPN
top_focus_8020.why: Domain 1 is 30% and half of it is networking; most traps (stateless NACL, non-transitive peering, gateway endpoint scope, unencrypted DX) live here. 5-6 questions.

top_focus_8020.topic: IAM policy types and Organizations: identity vs resource vs boundary vs SCP, roles and STS, Cognito pools, Identity Center
top_focus_8020.why: Evaluation logic and 'who grants vs who caps' is the backbone of Domain 1; 3-4 questions plus every security question assumes it.

top_focus_8020.topic: Encryption: KMS key types and rotation, S3 SSE modes, CloudHSM, Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store, ACM
top_focus_8020.why: Highly factual, fast to memorize, 3-4 questions; the SSE-KMS audit trail and Secrets Manager rotation facts alone recur constantly.

top_focus_8020.topic: EC2 purchasing options, Savings Plans, Spot, placement groups, Dedicated Hosts
top_focus_8020.why: Domain 4 (20%) leans on this: discount percentages, flexibility and the Spot interruption caveat. 3-4 questions with a deterministic decision table.

top_focus_8020.topic: Edge and DNS: CloudFront (OAC, signed URLs/cookies, Functions vs Lambda@Edge) vs Global Accelerator; Route 53 policies and health checks; DR strategies with RPO/RTO
top_focus_8020.why: Resilience (26%) uses Route 53 failover and DR ladder repeatedly; CloudFront vs GA is a guaranteed question. 4-5 questions.

top_focus_8020.topic: Load balancers and Auto Scaling (ALB/NLB/GWLB, health checks, target tracking vs step vs scheduled vs predictive) and Lambda/API Gateway limits
top_focus_8020.why: Standard three-tier scenarios; the tested facts are static IP (NLB), ELB health checks in ASG, Lambda 15 min / 10 GB, API Gateway 29 s. 3-4 questions.
